segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now we are going to start. Now we are going to talk for a little while. My name is Guy Soldier. My real name is Richard, but they call me Guy. I don’t know where it started. It started when I was little. I’m from up north. I don’t know if y’all ever been to Steely. It's close to Kenwood; that’s where I’m pastoring, at Steely, and now I’m going to ask y’all something. What is your name in English?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: GW.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: GW.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Beaver.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK. What about you? What's your name?
Livonia Buckhorn.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Buckhorn, Livonia Buckhorn. And what is your name?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Donald Adair.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Donald Adair. Donald Adair.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your Cherokee name?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Tsu-go-nud.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What’s your name?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: They call me by three names. ‘Ornery or rude Al.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born at?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I didn`t go to the doctor.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You didn’t? You were just born at home?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about you?
I understand it, but I don’t speak it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, alright.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: She’s just listening.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, she’s just listening. Oh, OK. She’s listening to y’all talk about each other. How about you? Where were you born?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: At Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You were born at the doctor there in Tahlequah? So, you just grew up there where you were born?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, towards Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s the same for you, too? You grew up in Greasy?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, I grew up in Greasy, too. My aunt, I mean my mom was his aunt. We're family.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, so y’all are family?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, we are both from Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you just grew up around there?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You didn’t go other places while you were growing up?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I went to the Army when I graduated, then we lived in Hawaii. That's where I met my wife. I went to Hawaii. That’s where I met my wife.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When she came from there, is that when y’all got married?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, we got married there in Hawaii.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She lived there in Hawaii?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We were married almost 40 years, then I lost her. How long has it been now?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: It’s been about three years now.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: That’s when she left.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s when she left? You said Hawaii. Did y’all live there for a while?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, we lived there for a while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was it like to live there? Was there a difference?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Not really, it was like they did the same thing we do around here. I told them we did the same thing they’re doing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They say it’s beautiful to live there. Is it really like that?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Oh yeah, it’s beautiful to live there. Everything was high.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The ocean was just right there, too, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: You could see it all the time. You could see it when you got up and you could see when you laid down.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some people say if you see the ocean all the time, it will make you sick. Did that happen to you?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: No, it didn’t, but when I finished and when her mom was giving us a house, I told them, “No, I`m going home,” and my wife said, “You don’t want it?” And I told her, “No, I don’t,” I told her, “I’m going home.” And she said, “Well, I'm going there, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, Praise the Lord. Y’all really loved each other when she came with you. How about you? Where did you use to live?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Just right there in Missouri. I went into the Army the year of 1973, just there in Missouri - Fort Leonard Wood. I finished there. I didn’t go anywhere else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you just grew up around there?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: But I tell them it would have been better back then. We didn’t hardly talk English. We grew up talking Cherokee, and we didn’t hardly understand it, or I didn’t hardly understand it back then. I would have gone somewhere else if I understood it, but it seemed like I didn’t want to go anywhere else. But now, I wish I would have known then what I know now, growing up back then and just finishing there. War was going on, too, the year of 1974, and they called up some people. Then they took us to the plane, but the leader told me my name wasn’t on the list and that I couldn’t go. I asked him, “How come? That’s what I asked for, to go in the Army.” Back then, you were the last one to be born. He told me he wasn’t going to send me. The leader told me I couldn’t go because I was the only boy left, and I told him, “That’s the reason I asked for this.” We were there arguing. I think about that sometimes. A couple of my buddies left at the same time. One of them got shot soon as he got there, and the other, five days later, on the fifth day, he got shot jumping out of a plane. When the leader heard that, he was telling me, because we were all supposed to be together. And he said, “If you was with them, you probably wouldn’t be alive.” And he said, “That’s the reason why I didn’t want you to go.” Their names are written on the wall where all the names are. My buddies’ names are on there. We were always together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How did you feel when they told you?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I felt hurt.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When your friends are having a hard time, you feel hurt, too, growing up with your buddies.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, we all practiced at the same time, and then they got called, but only a few of them came back. Those were the ones we always hung out with. We were always together when we were going to do something.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Like [unclear] John John Ross, we all grew up together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We all have the same grandpa and grandma.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We’re all family.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s real joyful when it’s like that.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: That’s what I tell them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s real joyful when it’s like that, and right now y’all are still together. It’s really joyful, but now most of them are gone. And you're saying your friends, most of them are gone, too. Sometimes I sit and think about them and think about when we were growing up. Is it the same with you?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, I think and wonder how it would have been.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: You know Roger Vann?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I think I do. I might have seen him around.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Him and us.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We all grew up together.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We all have the same grandpa and grandma. We played ball growing up.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I wonder how many windows we’ve broken when we were playing ball. We would get in trouble. They would get on to us, and they would put in a new window when they forgot about it, and then the window would be broken again after a while. We were just getting in trouble all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Have y’all ever stolen any watermelon?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I never stole anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time we were stealing watermelons, we were probably this tall [gesture], we gave him a watermelon at the fence. Then we took off running. He was right behind us with the watermelon, but after a while he fell and the watermelon busted.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I guess that’s what happens when you steal.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, something will happen.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That’s what I was telling them. When we were growing up, we never stayed in the house. We always stayed outside.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: You couldn’t sit by Grandpa.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: “Go outside. Go somewhere.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Especially when the elders came over.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: When a lot of people came over - I mean, a lot of people came over all the time, like on Saturdays and Sundays. We would be waiting to eat. I would be thinking, “I wish they would hurry up and leave before they eat everything up.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would let y’all eat last.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: They would let the visitors eat first.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: And then, at night, we would play ring toss.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We would hang rubbers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, them round rubbers.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, we would hang them at night. We'd be hollering around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they used to do, especially in the wintertime, or like when it snowed. That’s when they would gather, and they would brew coffee and they would throw.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Sometimes they would play hold 'em with cards. They called it hold 'em.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they called it hold ‘em.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We played cards. We played all night on Friday nights. Sometimes on Friday nights we’d go coon hunting at 12 with our Uncle Jack, and then we would walk around all night in the woods. We would be back around eight or nine.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: He would take you everywhere, and he would take you all night.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, he would. He would take you all night long.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was y’all doing with the raccoons?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Our grandma would cook them, but I don’t know how she did it. It was the fur, ‘cause they used to sell the fur. A long time ago, they used to pay good. We didn’t know, we were just going out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all were just like playing?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We never left around eight or nine. We left at 12 midnight to go hunting.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: What was it? Kerosene? We would carry kerosene lamps.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all have dogs?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I had one. It was a blue tick.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it a good one?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, it was a good one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time, where I’m from, they were bragging about the dogs they had then. They went hunting back then. I don’t know if y’all ever knew that. They said the dog was going crazy when it was drooling. Did y’all ever see that? One of them was a white man, and the other one was my wife’s uncle, and they went hunting and after a while the dog came back running and it was drooling, and they said, “It’s going crazy,” and they took off running. And the dog was just running behind, and the white man said there was a tree close by, and he grabbed onto a branch. Soon as he grabbed it, it broke. My uncle said he climbed up a tree, and he was up there laughing at him. His laugh got hard, and his mouth got stiff, so they had to call an ambulance. They took him to the doctor, laughing.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: So, they took him laughing?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was telling a funny story. That was my wife’s uncle telling about what happened.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Back when we were growing up, that’s all they would do is joke around.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They wouldn’t feel sorry for you.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: They wouldn’t feel sorry for you. Especially my uncle Tsu-so-lu-da, he was a liar. When he told something, he told it like it was true. We'd be listening like it was true.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When he started, y’all were beside him with y’all’s mouths open.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We had our necks stretched out when he told something. And Jack, our grandpa, he would say, “Huh-uuuun, you're lying. He’s lying. Y’all’s uncle lies a lot.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Here a while back, I was telling them there was someone named Radio where I’m from.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I’ve seen him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You seen him? He was real good at telling stories. He'd make it sound like it’s true, and you know it’s not true, but we still sit and listen.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That one used to like to lie. His name was Sesliy Feathers. I used to like to listen, but he was a liar, uh-huh.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Did you hear about that one when he went to Stilwell? Tell him about that one.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He said he was in Sallisaw. He said he had quite a bit to drink, and felt tired, and didn’t feel like walking. He said he was thinking, “I got to walk that far to Cherry Tree.” He said after a while, there was a train coming real slow. Then he said, “That train goes by my house, my mom’s house.” Then he said, “I took off running, and I jumped and I fell in a hole, and then it started going faster and faster. My feet were just smoking when I went by my mom’s house, and my mom was sitting outside.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: “I was tired when I got there.”

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He said, “My shoes were just smoking.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was telling them about Radio that I was talking about. One time, I was working for the county for about a year. It was noon, and all of us workers were sitting around. Radio pulled up. “Where you headed, Radio?” “Oh, I'm going fishing. I caught one the other day, a big fish it was, about this long.” “How much did it weigh, Radio?” “Well, the picture on there said it weighed five pounds.”

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Us, too, I think he was about our third uncle, Tom No-k-s. We'd go fishing sometimes on Saturdays. That old man, he liked to fish. When he would cast it out and if he wasn’t getting a bite, I would be watching him, and he would be doing this [gesture], and then after a while, he would yank his pole and he would say, “A huh-uuuum, I missed it.” And if he caught one this long [gesture], it would be this long [gesture].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Radio was funny. Radio was like that, too.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: How come they called him Radio?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He would lie about stuff.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He was a liar, too, I knew him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His real name was Earnest, but they named him Radio ‘cause he would tell stories, just making up stuff to tell. He already knew what to tell when you saw him.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Sesliy… There were people from Arkansas sitting in a bar, and Sesliy walked in. He walked by them, and they said, “Well, Sesliy, tell us a good one.” Sesliy said, “I can’t. My mom just passed away.” And just walked on by. After a while, they were still sitting there. They started thinking, so they decided to take some food to where his mom lived, and when they got there, Sesliy was sitting on one side and his mom on the other side. Then they said, “Sesliy, you told us your mom died.” Sesliy said, “Well, you told me to tell you a good one.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was just wanting food?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, he just got some food ‘cause he was a liar. Towards that way, I don’t know if anybody tells the truth.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Whenever they saw Radio coming, they would say, “Oh no.”

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That’s the way it is. That’s what I’m saying. When we were all growing up, it was really outside, sometimes we would be running around in the woods playing, and sometimes we would climb trees and bring them down. It’s amazing that we`re still alive.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We were acting like Tarzan.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We would hang off the grape vine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all ever smoke that grape vine?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, our grandpa caught us one time. He went to the store. It was me, you, Hyub, Da-az, Roger, and P.J. I can’t remember who all were there.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: It might have been Mack Bo.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Was Bo. We all seen that hole where we smoked. After a while, we were all walking around dizzy. Our grandpa didn’t say anything to us, we just hid it. He was walking straight towards us with his cane, laughing. He just walked by us. He knew we had already smoked it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He just laughed at y’all?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He already knew that we were dizzy walking around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about where you worked at growing up?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I finished work up in Tulsa. I worked 34 years, and I retired there at the post office.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you just walk around town?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: No, I just stayed in there. I didn’t do that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, so you just stayed in there, and separated them, and put them in there?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I would have been walking around lost, if I’d done that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You would have been putting them in the wrong place? It’s a big town now, isn’t it? Back then, the town wasn’t that big, was it?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: The towns are getting bigger. Like right here, it’s starting to get big. They’re building stores close by now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And back from where I`m from.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Food just keeps going up, too.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Do they still play ball up towards where you live?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they still do that sometimes. There’s some ball fields close to where we live, and they also have some tennis courts there, too, where they play tennis.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Do you go over there and chase tennis balls around, or do you go chase biscuits?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They throw biscuits around. I’ll probably have a heart attack if I try to play. Sometimes in the summertime, they have the lights on till midnight.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They do good?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they do good. Sometimes the grown-ups would be playing ball, too. They use that big one - what do they call it? Nerf ball or something, yeah. They play ball with that, them Cherokees. I wonder what they are doing when they play ball like that. And you’re supposed to run towards first base, but when they play this, they play it backwards. They run towards third base, then second base. I think to myself, “They must be playing ball lost.”

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: For real. Back when we were growing up, we really didn’t have anything. We were on foot, and when we went swimming, we walked, and when we came back, we were all sweaty after swimming.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They built a dam down at Greasy. They built the dam close to Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all had a swimming hole there?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We was always there.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: All of us Cherokees were hanging around where the water was coming out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you work at?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I drove those big trucks for 31 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you been all over the United States?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I’ve been to 38 states, and I wouldn’t want to go to that many places. I was telling my wife I’d get lost if we went somewhere. It's been about 13 or 14 years since they retired me, ‘cause I had a heart attack while I was driving a truck. I was only 55 years old when they retired me. They didn’t want me to drive anymore, so they took my CDL away from me and gave me back the regular driver's license. Now I can only drive cars, or at least I think I can.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about when you said when you used to drive trucks? You been all over the United States? What happened when they saw you somewhere and found out you were Cherokee? Did they talk to you nice or what?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they talked to me nice. Back then I had a beard, and some of them thought I was a Mexican when I got somewhere. When I got somewhere, when a Mexican talked to me, I would talk to them in Cherokee and say ski-gi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were they amazed when they found out you were Cherokee?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they were amazed. They would ask me if I still spoke Cherokee. I told them, “Yeah, I still speak it. I barely speak English.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would start asking you questions?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they were asking me questions, especially about when I went into the Army. I guess I took after my uncle Tsu-so-lu-da. When I was in the Army, they asked me, “How did you join the Army being Cherokee?” I told them, “Well, my grandpa had to OK it before I could join the Army.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How come?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: We still lived outside in tents. He was sitting there listening, and he said, “Huh, what did you have to do first?” I told him I had to starve myself for five days. So I starved myself for five days. The only thing my grandpa gave me was a knife. My grandpa said, “We're going to find out if you’re really a man, and if you really want to go, and if you’re really willing to do it.” He told me, “I’m going to give you this knife, and you’re going to have to find food for yourself in the woods.” They were sitting there listening to me lie to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And they believed you?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they believed me. There was this one black guy sitting there, and he asked me, “How did you do it?” I told him it wasn’t easy, and it was very hard back then, I told him, ‘cause my grandpa only gave me a pocketknife.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I bet their eyes were this big looking at you.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, I told him I was starving for five days. I told him my grandpa only gave me a pocketknife. I thought he was going to give me a big knife, but instead he gave me a pocketknife this long [gesture], and he told me, he said, “We’re going to find out if you’re really a man or not.”

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: The people from the east coast, they really will believe you. Like in New York, you can really lie to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I had a friend, but he’s passed away. He was the only Cherokee. He was with other tribes, and he became friends with white people. After a while, they hollered, “hey!” And they told him to go in there. They said, “We’re going over here. There’s an Indian in there. If y’all want to talk to him, go talk to him.” He said they were standing at the doorway. They had to pay to talk to him. We just came back out and we went drinking.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: There was this white boy, he asked me what his name was, and I told him, “You're white,” and I told him, “You're Yo-Neg.” He said, “That’s my name.” He was telling everybody his name was Yo-Neg.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I was telling them lies really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just anything?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: It was like it was true.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: We would lie to them real good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: When they start believing us, I tell a really long lie. I would say, “It was like this.” Whenever they would ask something.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about you? Do you have any kids?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I have three kids, two girls, they live in Texas, and the boy lives in Tulsa.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do they all have kids?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, they have kids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Are they doing good?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Yeah, they’re doing good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you have any grandkids?

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Seven of them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Seven?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That’s it? I almost have the world filled up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know if y’all ever got to know Woody Hair?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He`s the same way, too.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I got my phone right here when we was talking about them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Woody Hair School. The kids were going to Woody Hair. It was up in Kenwood. One time, the Kenwood teacher asked them orite kids, “Who’s the father of our country?” One of the kids raised their hand. Teacher asked, “Who is it?” and the student said, “Woody Hair.” He had kids, but I don't know how many he had. He’s got a lot of grandkids, too.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I have 13 grandkids and eight great-grandkids, fixing to be nine. They're just coming out everywhere.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: It’s the Chief`s birthday today.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: It’s my birthday today. I guess I’m the Chief.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is it your birthday today?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s my birthday today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How old are you? You`re not keeping it a secret, are you?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m 18. I’m 67.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: 67, boy, happy birthday. Happy birthday.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Wa-do Wa-do. It was fun when we was growing up, that’s what I`m saying. I mean, we grew up rough, too. Right now, everything is going up, even food. It’s just that big, and the price of it is high. The food is getting low, but the price of it is going up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I remember.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: When we were growing up, everything was beans and corn.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Jack was my uncle, and Tsu-so-lu-da.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They were growing potatoes. I used to eat them.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: It seems like it’s just family. They didn’t use a tractor or horses.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: He had horses.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: They would use horses to plow. They would plow about 10 or more acres. They would grow potatoes, beans for the family to eat, and even corn. I was telling them if we had good heads on our shoulders, we would have been rich. They said, “How?” I said, “Well, they used to grow beans and then they would sell them a long time ago. They used to sell them at the canning factory in Stilwell.” They grew green beans, but like I said, they were only using horses when they plowed. And the pickers, we were the pickers. The whole family was benefiting from it. Back then, like I was telling him, back then when we were growing up, family was family.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s true.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: And now we look at each other hateful. Nowadays, when someone has $10, they’re rich. When they start working somewhere and start making a good amount of money, they forget they’re Cherokee and where they grew up and where they’re from. I told them I wouldn’t forget. I won’t forget how I was raised. We ate squirrel, rabbit, and deer. We didn’t kill them for fun back then. That’s what I miss sometimes - cornbread and squirrel.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Our grandma would catch chickens real fast.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, real fast.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My grandma would tell us, “Go catch that chicken,” whenever we went over there. And we would start chasing the chickens around, and when we caught it, we did the same thing. Then my mom and my grandma would fix them. Then we would eat dumplings.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That, too. I didn’t know what it was - my aunt probably knew what it was. My aunt Lyda, she used to do the cooking. When a lot of people came over on Saturdays, she would cook everything. She had a big plate while she was cooking, like beans and potatoes. She had a big cast iron pot to cook in. And bread.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: She would make a lot of bread.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, she didn’t use a gas stove, she used a wood stove. Sometimes she would have two about this long [gesture], for cooking bread and coffee. Like I was saying, when the visitors come over, they would feed them first, and like I was saying, I wanted to eat, too, before they ate the food up.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: A lot of people would come over all the time.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: And Grandpa, our grandpa that we talk about too, 80 or 70 years old. And he would still dive in when he went swimming. While he was fishing, we would be swimming. He would be sitting over there with just his pole, and he would be catching them there. We would be hollering around and he`d be catching them. He would be catching catfish. That’s all he caught and when he was done fishing, he would swim with us. Sometimes, - wait, he was about 80, or maybe past 90, and he would walk fast to the store with his cane.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: He would go after for some Pepsi.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, he would go after some Pepsi. I told him we’re not even that old. We're barely 60 years old, and we’re barely walking.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They had our grandpa in the Tulsa World newspaper.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What’s his name?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Di-ga-no-tsa-tli was his Cherokee name, and in English, it was James Vann.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, I remember seeing and reading that.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: When he was walking down the road, I called him the oldest Pepsi generation.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did he use to hunt, too?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember seeing that and reading it.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, that was our grandpa. Last time he killed one was back in ‘91 or ‘92. They just went by the house. He killed around there. But like I`m saying, that won’t happen anymore.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: All the time we would go maybe three or four times, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Store.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Just to go look for Pepsi. He was probably about 90 years old back then. He had to go on the highway for a little while, and a big truck went by him, and that wind knocked him down. That’s when somebody stopped by and told him, “You ain’t going to go no more.” And when we would head to town, he would get a big Pepsi.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: My grandpa was very funny, I still remember. There was a dog laying around outside where they were sitting, and he said, “Boy, I wouldn’t never want that dog to come inside the house.” The dog’s name was Buffalo, and he said he never would think to go inside, but soon as he got through talking, it went inside. “Aw, Duffalo, Duffalo, Duffalo!” His name was Duffalo now, instead of Buffalo.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about when your parents were still alive, and your grandkids? They didn’t tell y’all anything about the old Cherokees from North Carolina when we moved down here? They didn’t tell y’all anything about how some of them made it down here?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Just a little bit. They didn’t always tell us how it was on their way down here, but they told us they lost family on their way down here. When they made it down here, they were given some land, but I really don’t know, ‘cause our grandma was just a little girl. Grandma Grandpa – my grandma was 101 or 102 when she passed, and they said Grandpa was 109 when he passed away. He passed away in 1970.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: It was around there.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Grandma passed just after he did. Grandma was just laying in bed ‘cause she broke her hip. She broke her hip and she didn’t want to go to the doctor. Plus, the doctors said she was too old, and they couldn’t do anything, so she was just laying down all the time. But Grandpa, he still… when we lost Grandpa it wasn’t in a hospital. I never heard of Grandpa being in a hospital before. It was outside his house. When he jumped off, he missed a step and fell down, and got a cut on his head. That’s when they took him and he just went down after that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My sister married this man she got. My sister’s husband had a grandparent, and she was 90, almost 100 years, old and she would walk to church. There was a steep hill going up to the church, and she would be walking up it. Then when she passed away, they looked for the year she was born and they found it, too, and they figured out how old she was - 114 years old. But they said she was fixing something. She was peeling potatoes and when she got done, she told them she was going to lay down and rest. She went and laid down and that’s when she passed away. And when they went to go get the body the bones were breaking. I guess where they were, her body was so old.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: That’s how old she was?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Our grandpa, he was from tsa-tso/Georgia. There was a rich guy, his name was Joe, I think it was his grandpa. I think it was like the second or third generation from that way.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: They say they started the Trail of Tears at their home.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: You know where Dwight Mission is? My grandpa’s grandpa started all those missions that are there. There was a mansion in Georgia, and across from it was a mission. That’s where he started, and then they started building those everywhere, like the one at Dwight Mission. He was a wealthy man. We should be wealthy, too, instead of sitting here poor. Back then, they weren’t supposed to hire a white man as a treasurer, but they hired a white man. That’s when it started. They chased him out of that house and the government took it. But he built another one just like it towards Webber’s Falls, but it burnt down. The river boats were his, too, and he had a lot of things. He had about 200-400 black slaves. Those houses they have in Georgia, they were built by those slaves. The rock house, they built it by themselves. That’s how far… Me, on my Adair side, they’re from Georgia, too. They're from Adairsville, Georgia. It’s my fourth grandpa. He started building stores. He built a town. They were white people. They were Scottish. My grandpa came from that way, but as time went on, he had boys and girls - there were about 11 of them. They started getting them women from the Cherokee, and the white man side. My grandpa, he was full Adair on the Adair side, but on that side he was white. Them white Adairs that live around here, were kin to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, it’s amazing when you think about it.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, it is amazing. It’s like what I was telling you, my dad, he grew up working in the fields, plowing, and doing carpentry helping a white guy. His name was Dick Banes. He was getting paid 50 cents an hour, working all day long. But back then, things didn’t cost that much. He would start at eight, sometimes at seven, and he would bring him back around four or five in the evening. He worked that hard, but we still had shoes on, and we had clothes on. And in the summertime, he would go to Colorado to go cut broom corn. He went to work that way, and when he came back, he had a little bit of money. At [unclear] or what they call it it was [unclear] Your dad, he fought in WW2, too, ain’t it? And my dad fought in WW2. My dad never talked about it. He never told us about stuff like that when we were growing up, what he saw, what happened. He never told it. He passed away, and I don’t know what happened there. He couldn’t speak English. Some couldn’t speak English and couldn’t understand it. Sometimes I wonder, “How did they ever make it?”

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I never heard Grandma and Grandpa talking English.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: No, they spoke Cherokee all the time.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: When we went to school, we didn’t speak English.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: No, we always spoke Cherokee. We got in trouble when we did, especially when I started lying. We was just getting in trouble. Back then, they were saying, “Y’all have to learn English here at school.” They said, “Not Cherokee, y’all are going to learn English.” They tell us, “Y’all are going to learn English. Y’all ain’t going to use Cherokee anymore,” and we went to school at Greasy. Sometimes I wonder why they want to learn Cherokee now. Back then we couldn’t hardly talk English, and we couldn’t hardly understand it. And now I wonder why? That’s what I tell them, growing up in Greasy we talk different but up towards north like Jay and Kenwood, they talk different, too, or like towards Belfonte and like here in Tahlequah and like Cherry Tree, they talk different but we still understand each other. The dialects are different but we still know what they are talking about. I was telling them, when you tell a white man something you know what you're talking about, especially if you're full blood; whatever you're saying, whatever you're talking about, and if they put it in a different way, that’s what they will use. They won’t believe a truly Indian went through and what they said; that’s what I`m saying: you talk different and I talk different, but we still understand each other. And now, if they do one thing, that’s how the law is. They are making everything different, and something else over here is not just one law. I told them if y’all can put it as one, we can all understand each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like, how you were saying dig-too-lan is that how most say it?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Some call it tsa-tla-di-tla.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And up north, they call it doe-leel.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: See, that’s what I'm saying: we understand each other what it is. That makes three. When they talk about it, they use one of them; which one are they using? It’s better if they just tell them; if they can put that all together, they would know. They would definitely know Cherokee and how a person can understand someone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes it really does happen that way, and sometimes you have to think about what they are saying, and then later on you'll catch it. And it’s like how you're saying, sometimes you do have to think about how we talk. I went to Belfonte for a little while; I pastored there, and then back to Jay, and they were talking different, but I was understanding them a little bit.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: It’s like how I was saying in Bell… Towards Bell they talk slow. Belfonte kinda talks the same way, but there is a little bit of difference between them. I was telling them you can probably understand someone from Bell. They asked me how I understand them. I said I can speak the same language as Bell. And, like ball they call it playing ball.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what they call it up North, playing ball. They also say Do y’all play sports that’s how they say playing ball, too, or they will say do y’all play ball.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Or they would say y’all play ball, it’s just like what I was saying; everything is that way. If you really talk about it, I really enjoy being around people who talk Cherokee. Sometimes there’s some; I don’t make fun of them. The white people will say, “Siyo,” and that’s all they know. I say siyo back. I say, “Are y’all doing OK back from where y’all grew up?” Sometimes they'll turn around and say, “That’s all I know.” I tell them, “If that’s all you can say, it’s better if you just say hi.” I told them, “I thought you were going to talk Cherokee when you said that.” That one time it was funny - remember when I told you they thought I was Mexican? One time we were in Wal-Mart walking around. This old man walked by and said, “Uh-hum, this Mexican is walking around in the way.” And he was talking about me. I didn’t say anything to him. We met again and he said, “Huh-hum, here comes that Mexican again.” I asked him “Where do you see a Mexican?” He said, “Heeey, He was calling me Mexican ‘cause of my mustache. He said, “I didn’t know you spoke Cherokee.”

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: It`s real good that the kids are learning how to speak Cherokee. They're doing good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, we’ve lost a lot of Cherokee.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, we have lost a lot of Cherokee. See, the kids, they should talk to them all the time when they can understand it. But I don’t know if I wanted them to talk Cherokee all the time, because back then, the elders didn’t understand English and the white man took stuff from them. That’s why I told them that I… “How come you don’t speak fluent Cherokee, and your wife understands everything in Cherokee? How come you didn’t teach your kids?” I told them, “Well, my grandma and grandpa and my uncles all of them didn’t understand English. They lost a lot of things just ‘cause they didn’t understand it, and the Cherokee that could understand English, and the Cherokee translator, was taking everything that he cheated the Cherokees out of.” That’s what I told them the Cherokee children… I said, “That’s why I want y’all to talk English the best way y’all can and understand it. I don’t want the white man to come from behind and steal from y’all. That’s the reason why the elders lost some things, just ‘cause they didn’t understand English.” That’s why I told them I didn’t want anybody to have anything and be taking away from them. That’s how far I thought about it, and now they want Cherokee speakers sometimes. I also wonder why, ‘cause we lost enough already. When they started doing this Cherokee Speakers, I asked you know to help them teach to speak Cherokee. I told them I can’t write Cherokee and I can’t read it, but I know what Cherokee is. I know how it is. They told me, “We can't put you in and teach.” I asked them how come and they told me, “You have to go to school first before you can come.” I asked them, “Why do I need to go to school? I`m already Cherokee. I should be teaching them.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Here at Cherokee Nation, there’s one that’s part Cherokee. They go to church. He asked his mom one time, his mom is full-blood Cherokee, how come you didn’t teach me how to speak Cherokee? And she said, “Son, I didn’t want you to go through the hardship that I went through when I was going to school speaking Cherokee. I had it hard. I didn’t want that to happen to you.” He asked, “How come you didn’t teach me just a little bit?” And she told him, “I felt sorry for you.” That’s what the Cherokees went through; that's why they speak English. And how their parents went through like what you were saying how they was getting robbed.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: And getting cheated. My mom didn’t speak it. She didn’t try to speak it, but her grandkids knew what their grandma wanted. When them boys said something… When she said something, they would do it. So I asked them, “How do y’all understand what y’alls grandma is saying when she says it in Cherokee?” They said, “When she points, we know what she’s saying. That’s what we watch for - where she points.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about, let’s say like food? Your kids and family, what is y’alls favorite food to eat right now? It’s changed since last year.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: I still like to eat gravy and I like wild onion. I like what they call poke salad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: DLA-DE.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: DLA-DE.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: And I like to eat that fire crest, or what they call that, better than poke salad. Pour a little lard especially if you put a little salt and baking grease on it. Pour that on there, and hot dog, you’d be eating like dogs, saying tlaop-tlaop-tlaop.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But they don’t make stuff like that anymore.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: I watch those cooking shows on TV sometimes when they’re cooking. When they start using that grease, they use that lard cause they want taste.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That lard is some good stuff. We still use that lard.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: What kind of grease? It’s just grease, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they just called it grease. They would go buy five gallons of it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My mom gets a tin one this big [gesture].

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That was five gallons.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And a bag of flour.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: They would take 25 pounds or 50 pounds, and they would take 100 pounds of potatoes to last them a month.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what we did for a month. And in the springtime, they would plant potatoes, and then they would dig them up, and they would put them in the cellar so they wouldn’t spoil.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: That’s different now. You know what they call that smoker? When my grandpa killed a pig, when they killed a pig, he would hang in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, what they call a smokehouse.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He would have a lot of salt on it. And it would just hang there, and if they wanted meat, they would just go cut some off. But it'll hang there just a little while and it’d be rotten. That’s how much difference there is today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Or if you have a dog, they’ll eat it up.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, they will steal it and be dragging it off. That’s what I was saying. It’s funny - when I first took my first ex-wife, I told her, “They have dogs at my grandma’s that can sing.” She said, “Huh-uh!” I said, “They have dogs that can sing.” So I asked her, “Do you want to go?” She said, “I'd like to see.” We got there and they were sitting around outside. After a while, three mangy dogs with no fur came and sat by us. One started high, and the other one started low. “I told you they could sing, but you can’t hear them,” I told her. One would start low, and the other one would be like a fiddle, high. That one from Moody, you know him, that Tony Mouse?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He was funny. Tony Mouse, they said Tony Mouse got rich. I said how come, and they said, “He's got baby elephants.” Where'd he get them? I don’t know. He was real rich. He had baby elephants. People believed it, and went up there, and when they got there, they had mangy dogs. They had the mangiest puppies there, calling them baby elephants. Tony was rich.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That one time, people come to where I’m from. They were looking for an elder person. They told them he lives by a couple of houses. He said, “How can I tell which house he lives in?” They told him, “You will see colored dogs.” They called them pink dogs ‘cause they had no fur.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: One of my friends, he lived in Cherry Tree, and he had a dog. What’s its name - understand? That’s what its name was, Understand. Huh? What’s its name – understand. Is it Spot? Understand! Huh? Is it Blue? Understand! He started getting mad and said, “What’s the name of the dog?” “I’m telling you its name - Understand.” We almost started arguing. I was telling him its name was Understand and he was still sitting there.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: Them boys were talking about it. There was a man named Ook-sann. They called him that all the time, but he knew his name. He said, “Y’all boys come over. We'll go hunting.” They said they showed up to his house and he said, “I didn’t want to say that.” His wife came out. I didn’t want to call him Ook-sann. Cherokee was his real name. I asked her, “Is Cherokee home?” His wife turned around and said, “Hey, Ook-sann, they want you out here.” That’s what his name was?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what his name was, Ook-sann. When he was growing up, every time he said something, he would be saying, “Jak-sann jak-sann jak-sann,” so they just named him Ook-sann.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: That’s what his name was.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: Yeah, his name was Cherokee, but he would say Ook-sann, so they named him Ook-sann. We really have funny names, the ones that grew up that way.

segments.speaker: g-w-beaver
segments.translation: His wife turned around and said, “Hey, Ook-sann, they're looking for you out here.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back where I’m from, there was a guy named Dave Guess, but he’s not alive anymore. He went for a physical for the Army in Oklahoma City. “Alright, chief, what’s your name?” “Guess.” “What’s your name?” “Guess.” “Chief, I’m getting tired of playing games with you. What’s your name?” Guess, that was his name.

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: My uncle Tsu-so-lu-da was talking about it. He never did a physical with the Army, but it funny when he tells it. He said, “We were in line naked, without clothes on. They told one of them to bend over. He bent over and they checked him out, and they told him, “We can’t take you.” He asked how come? They told him, “There’s something green growing out of you.” He ate wild onion and poke salad, and he had some green stuff on his butt. They told him they couldn’t take him cause he had some green stuff on his butt, so they ran him off. Then there was another one, they told him they couldn’t take him. He asked why, and they told him, “There’s something yellow coming out of you.” And it was corn. He was going to lie, especially when he done that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Have you ever heard of or seen Guy Sapp?

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He was a liar.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time I made a garden. I planted onion, potatoes, and beans. After a while, I heard somebody talking towards my garden. I thought, “Boy, somebody might be stealing from me.” I went around there and they kept talking. I was looking around and saying, “Where they talking at?” I looked towards my garden again. They were talking there at my garden. The potatoes I planted there, them potatoes were talking to each other, saying, “Move over, move over!”

segments.speaker: donald-adair
segments.translation: He loved to tell stories. He was real funny. It was towards Jay he got him an Indian woman. The Indian man got him a white woman, but that white had a little boy. Then she started making gravy, and that little boy was watching her make the gravy. Then after she was finished making the gravy, the boy asked, “How do you know if the gravy is good?” She said, “Well, boy when it starts going blop blop blop.” There was a preacher one time, he wasn’t married. Then one day he wanted a woman to get married. He didn’t want to be by himself. Going around preaching, he came to a tree and started praying, saying, “My Lord, I want you to bring me a wife for both of us to do the right thing, to do your work. I want you to bring me a wife.” Then he said Amen. He didn’t know there was a hoot owl behind him. It said, “Who?” Then he said, “Eeeeeee!” Then he took off running. That’s what I’m going to say, “Who?” When it says “who?” I’m going to say “Eeeeeee!”
